rationale: Today's slate has 5 pieces, all on GLP-1 medicines, in line with the 10-16 playbook. The long video (L1) explains orforglipron. Explainers about named new drugs are the only long videos that get views for us. Its hook is the EU drug committee's (CHMP's) positive opinion on Oct 16. The body uses published trials: ATTAIN-1 in NEJM (2025), ACHIEVE-1 and ACHIEVE-3. Because the evidence is settled, it should pass the fact-check, and it doesn't repeat the 9-28 menopause angle or the 9-29 pill comparison. S1 is a spin-off of L1 that picks up the breaking EU news. S2 is the stomach side effects follow-up to the SURMOUNT-5 Short, which got 109 views on day 1. Head-to-heads naming both drugs work, tirzepatide is in the title, and it uses different data from the 10-15 weight Short. S3 is a calm 'what's confirmed vs not' warning about compounded and counterfeit GLP-1s, a format that has worked for us. It covers a fresh story (the Bloomberg inspection report, the MHRA seizure and the photo-review study) and is different from the 10-16 retatrutide Reddit Short. The carousel is a save-worthy myth-buster on supplements sold as 'GLP-1'. Note that carousels have reached only 0–3 accounts so far, so it's the lowest-stakes slot. Mix: 2 emerging or rising news pieces (S1, S3), 2 evergreen pieces with a timely hook (L1, S2) and 1 myth-buster (C1). No pillar is used more than twice. Skipped today: bootleg retatrutide (covered 10-16), stopping a GLP-1 (weak on YouTube and covered 10-13), and the retatrutide long video (TRIUMPH-2 covered 9-30).

pieces.topic: Orforglipron (Foundayo): how the first non-peptide, small-molecule GLP-1 pill works, and what its Phase 3 trials showed
pieces.angle: Hook (≤15 s): 'On Oct 15, 2026, the EU medicines committee (CHMP) recommended approving orforglipron (Foundayo) for weight management and type 2 diabetes. EMA published this on Oct 16, and the European Commission's final decision is pending. The FDA approved it for chronic weight management on Apr 1, 2026.' Body as planned. The food/water point is credited to the US prescribing information. 'First approved non-peptide GLP-1 pill.' ATTAIN-1 gives per-arm results vs placebo, with group sizes and estimand from NEJM, and no mapping to marketed strengths. ACHIEVE-1 (NEJM 2025) and ACHIEVE-3 (Lilly reported, vs Rybelsus 14 mg) each come with their own population. The side effects beat includes discontinuation vs placebo and the boxed thyroid warning. Comparison with the semaglutide pill: separate trials, no ranking. Prescriber questions, no dosing or switching. Prescriber line.
pieces.working_title: Orforglipron (Foundayo): How Does a Non-Peptide GLP-1 Pill Work? What the Trials Show
pieces.why: Explainers on named new drugs are the only long videos that travel (median about 30 vs 2.5 for approved drugs). Today's EU news is the hook, and the body rests on peer-reviewed NEJM trials that can be checked in depth. | fact-check: Topic is sound and well within policy. I checked: FDA approved Foundayo (orforglipron) on Apr 1, 2026 for chronic weight management in adults with obesity, or overweight with at least 1 weight-related condition. Sources: Lilly/BioSpace press release https://www.biospace.com/press-releases/fda-approves-lillys-foundayo-orforglipron-the-only-glp-1-pill-for-weight-loss-that-can-be-taken-any-time-of-day-without-food-or-water-restrictions and Consultant360 https://www.consultant360.com/fda-alerts/fda-approves-orforglipron-foundayo-chronic-weight-management. The CHMP positive opinion was ADOPTED 15 Oct 2026 and published by EMA on 16 Oct 2026, so the angle's 'Oct 16' date is wrong. Sources: https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/human/EPAR/foundayo and https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/news/meeting-highlights-committee-medicinal-products-human-use-chmp-12-15-october-2026. The European Commission decision is still pending. The recommended EU indication is BOTH type 2 diabetes AND weight management (BMI ≥30, or 27 to <30 with at least 1 weight-related comorbidity). Fixes needed: (1) Date correction above. (2) The EMA summary of opinion does NOT mention food or water timing. Attribute 'any time of day, without food or water restrictions' to the US prescribing information (FDA label), not to EMA. (3) Say 'first approved non-peptide/small-molecule GLP-1 pill', not just 'first' (other small molecules, e.g. danuglipron, were tested and dropped). (4) The side-effects beat must include the US label's boxed warning on thyroid C-cell tumours (do not use with personal or family history of MTC or MEN2). Use EMA's 'most common side effects are gastrointestinal such as nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea'. (5) Never map ATTAIN-1 trial doses (6/12/36 mg) to the marketed strengths. Reports list US strengths as 0.8–17.2 mg, so they are not interchangeable. Give trial-arm results only, with no strength or dose guidance. (6) ATTAIN-1 has a 12.4% vs 0.9% placebo figure (top dose, 72 wk). Take each arm's figure, estimand and group sizes from the NEJM paper itself. (7) ACHIEVE-3: check whether a peer-reviewed paper now exists. If not, every number is 'Lilly reported (topline, date)'. Label the comparator 'oral semaglutide (Rybelsus) 14 mg', not 'the Wegovy pill'. (8) Performance note from the playbook: approved-drug long-forms have a median of 2.5 views, and pills are advised as Shorts. Consider whether this long-form slot is worth it.

pieces.topic: Orforglipron gets an EU green light: how is this GLP-1 pill different?
pieces.angle: Answer by 10 s: 'It's a small-molecule pill, not a peptide. Its US label says you can take it any time of day without food or water rules.' ATTAIN-1: 12.4% average weight loss on the highest trial dose vs 0.9% on placebo over 72 weeks, in adults with obesity or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes (group sizes in narration). Status line: 'EU medicines committee recommended approval Oct 15, 2026 (published Oct 16); final European Commission decision pending; US-approved for weight management Apr 1, 2026.' Side effects line: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea. 'Follow for more.' Prescriber line.
pieces.working_title: Orforglipron Pill Gets EU Backing: How Is It Different? #shorts
pieces.why: Spin-off of L1. It brings the breaking CHMP news into a Short, and pill explainers have done well on both YouTube and Instagram (55 and 52). | fact-check: Facts check out with corrections. The CHMP opinion was adopted Oct 15, 2026 and published Oct 16 (https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/human/EPAR/foundayo). EMA's summary of opinion does not mention food or water. That claim comes from the US label and Lilly (https://www.biospace.com/press-releases/fda-approves-lillys-foundayo-orforglipron-the-only-glp-1-pill-for-weight-loss-that-can-be-taken-any-time-of-day-without-food-or-water-restrictions), so 'per EMA' must go. The EU recommendation covers obesity/overweight AND type 2 diabetes. ATTAIN-1 number to use: 12.4% average weight loss on the highest dose (36 mg) vs 0.9% on placebo at 72 weeks, in adults with obesity or overweight with a weight-related condition, without diabetes. Confirm the figure and group sizes against NEJM. Say 'highest dose in the trial' rather than naming mg, to avoid implying a marketed strength or dose. Title 'Gets EU Backing' is fine. Never write 'EU approved' or 'green light' on screen without 'recommended'. Side effects line: mostly stomach-related (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea) per EMA.

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide vs semaglutide: which had more stomach side effects in SURMOUNT-5?
pieces.angle: Title: 'Tirzepatide vs Semaglutide: Which Had More Stomach Side Effects?' Answer by 10 s: 'In SURMOUNT-5, stomach side effects were about as common on both.' Then nausea, diarrhoea, constipation and vomiting rates per arm, plus GI-related stopping rates per arm, all from NEJM, with group sizes. Say side effects weren't a formally tested comparison. Population: adults with obesity, no diabetes, 72 weeks, open-label, Lilly-funded. 2 recommended habits (smaller meals eaten slowly; fluids unless you've been told to limit fluids). 'Don't switch or stop on your own.' Prescriber line.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide vs Semaglutide: Which Had More Stomach Side Effects? #shorts
pieces.why: A follow-up to the 109-view SURMOUNT-5 head-to-head. It names both drugs with tirzepatide first, and it's the strongest bet for the 08:00 slot. | fact-check: Good, data-backed head-to-head (SURMOUNT-5, Aronne et al., NEJM 2025; 72 wk; adults with obesity without diabetes; open-label; Lilly-sponsored; max tolerated doses). The stomach side-effect rates were broadly SIMILAR between arms. Secondary summaries report roughly nausea 44% vs 44%, diarrhoea 23% vs 23%, constipation 27% vs 29%, and vomiting 15% on tirzepatide vs 21% on semaglutide. Do NOT use these secondary numbers: take every rate and the GI-discontinuation rates (with group sizes, ~374 vs ~376) directly from the NEJM paper or its supplement. Adverse events were not a formally tested endpoint. The title question must be answered honestly as 'about the same overall', with no claim that one drug is 'gentler' or 'better tolerated'. Vomiting can be mentioned only as a numerical difference, not a tested one. Note the timing (mostly during dose escalation) only if the paper says so. Habits are fine as 'recommended', with the fluid caveat. Keep 'Don't switch or stop on your own'.

pieces.topic: Is your semaglutide or tirzepatide the real thing? Compounded and counterfeit GLP-1s: what's confirmed
pieces.angle: 'Compounded and counterfeit GLP-1s aren't the same thing. Here's what's confirmed.' (1) Branded semaglutide/tirzepatide are FDA-approved. Compounded versions are not FDA-approved or reviewed. (2) Bloomberg reported on Oct 15, 2026 that FDA inspectors found mould and falsified records at 2 overseas plants making ingredients for compounded versions, now on import alert. (3) UK: on Oct 14, 2026, MHRA and police seized over 12,000 fake tirzepatide and retatrutide pens (GOV.UK). (4) In one US online survey (Obesity Science & Practice, primary URL), photos showed 25.8% were on compounded products, and most of them believed they were on a brand. Close: ask your prescriber or pharmacist which product you're on; don't stop or change your medicine on your own. Prescriber line.
pieces.working_title: Is Your Semaglutide or Tirzepatide the Real Thing? What's Confirmed #shorts
pieces.why: Calm warnings about gray-market products are a lane that works for us (165 and 58). Tirzepatide is in the title, and the rising news this week is a fresh story, separate from the 10-16 retatrutide piece. | fact-check: Sources exist. (a) Bloomberg, Oct 15, 2026: https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-15/compound-semaglutide-tirzepatide-plants-in-china-found-with-black-mold-by-fda reports FDA inspectors found mould, contamination and falsified records at 2 Chinese plants making semaglutide/tirzepatide ingredients for compounding, and FDA placed both on import alert. Attribute it as 'Bloomberg reported that FDA inspectors found…'. Do not name the plants. (b) MHRA on GOV.UK: 'Counterfeit weight loss pens worth £2 million seized by MHRA and West Midlands Police' https://www.gov.uk/government/news/counterfeit-weight-loss-pens-worth-2-million-seized-by-mhra-and-west-mids-police (Oct 14, 2026; >12,000 fake retatrutide and tirzepatide pens, Birmingham). Specify UK, the date, and that retatrutide isn't approved anywhere. (c) The Obesity Science & Practice photo study exists (322 US adults from an online research panel, Oct 2025–Jan 2026; 83 = 25.8% on compounded products by photo; about two-thirds of those reported a brand-name drug). It is confirmed only via Medscape (paywalled). The scriptwriter MUST cite the Wiley/PubMed primary URL. If no primary URL can be found, drop the stat. Say 'in one US online survey', since the sample isn't representative. Keep COMPOUNDED (legal in some circumstances, not FDA-approved) clearly separate from COUNTERFEIT (fake, illegal). Never imply that compounded = counterfeit, or that pharmacy-dispensed branded pens are likely fake. Calm tone, no emoji, no sellers or prices, no tips on spotting fakes that read as buying guidance.

pieces.topic: 'GLP-1 supplements' vs GLP-1 medicines: what's the difference, and evidence-based ways to support your own GLP-1
pieces.angle: Slide 1: 'Do GLP-1 supplements work like semaglutide or tirzepatide?' Slide 2: the medicines were tested in large RCTs (STEP-1, 68 wk; SURMOUNT-1, 72 wk; adults with obesity or overweight plus a condition, without diabetes). Slide 3: 'GLP-1' supplements aren't FDA-approved drugs and haven't been shown in large trials to match these results. Slides 4–6: protein, fibre, and vegetables or protein before carbs, each 'linked to a higher GLP-1 response after meals in small studies', each healthy habits, not replacements, with source tags. Include the kidney caveat and 'build fibre up gradually'. Slide 7: prescriber questions. Last slide: disclaimer plus prescriber line.
pieces.working_title: GLP-1 Supplements vs GLP-1 Medicines: What's Actually Different?
pieces.why: A rising consumer search with few careful explainers so far, and a list format people save. It's also the bold myth-buster slot. | fact-check: Safe, on-pillar myth-buster, but it needs tighter scope. (1) Supplements: say that products sold as 'GLP-1 supplements' are not FDA-approved drugs and have not been shown in large randomized trials to produce weight loss comparable to semaglutide or tirzepatide. Do NOT say they 'don't work' or 'are dangerous' without a source. Name no products or ingredients. (2) STEP-1 = adults with obesity or overweight with a weight-related condition, without diabetes, 68 wk. SURMOUNT-1 = the same population, without diabetes, 72 wk. (3) Food-habit evidence is mostly small, short meal-test studies, e.g. the food-order study by Shukla et al. in Diabetes Care 2015 was in about 11 people with type 2 diabetes. These show higher post-meal GLP-1 or lower glucose, not weight loss. Say 'linked to a higher GLP-1 response after meals in small studies', and state that the effect is far smaller than the medicines and does not replace them. Every tag must point to a primary source that says exactly that. (4) Keep the kidney caveat for protein and 'build fibre up gradually with fluids'. (5) Playbook: carousels reach 0–3. Consider rebuilding this as a Short ('Do GLP-1 supplements work like tirzepatide?').
